Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation

I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me

issues.item: Triggers: Pregnancy/Birth Reminders: Pregnancy, childbirth, or babies in general
issues.explanation: Pregnancy/birth reminders are hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of physical abuse by a romantic partner in this 34-year-old male unless there is unreported trauma content involving pregnancy, childbirth, or infants. The other trigger items point toward sexualized/interpersonal threat and hospital-associated reminders, making this item the clearest trauma-incongruent outlier.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Checking Locks: repeatedly check locks, doors, or windows
issues.explanation: Repeated lock-checking is more suggestive of fear of external intrusion/burglary than trauma-specific coping with partner physical abuse, and it is weakly connected to the rest of the profile. The other maladaptive strategies reflect interpersonal avoidance and affect suppression, whereas this item introduces a different safety concern.

issues.item: Threat: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: This threat item duplicates compulsive checking behavior rather than describing a perceived current threat state, and it implies fear of break-in/external danger that is not otherwise supported by the trauma narrative, appraisals, or memory content. In combination with the matching maladaptive strategy item, it forms an internally coherent pair but one that is poorly integrated with the rest of the formulation.

vignette: Kwame, a 34‑year‑old African American parole officer, recalls the night that turned his life into a series of alarms. He was home with his girlfriend when she began to shout and shove him, the sharp sting of her broken glass echoing in the kitchen. Blood spattered the countertop, and the scent of it laced the air with a metallic chill. He fled to the car, only to find himself surrounded by neighbors who called 911. The ambulance’s antiseptic odor wafted over his shoulder as the paramedics ushered him into a sterile waiting room. That smell has since become a constant reminder of the violence that once shook his world. The hospital’s antiseptic fragrance, the sight of men in uniforms, and the feeling of being scrutinized as if a man had to look over his shoulder all trigger Kwame’s acute threat response. When he hears the buzz of the monitor or sees a male officer at his desk, his body tightens, muscles tense, ready to spring. The same moments bring back auditory memories of his girlfriend’s scream, the hiss of her voice, and a taste that feels like the metallic tang of blood. These memories are vivid enough that he often feels as though the assault is replaying in real time, his mind refusing to distinguish past from present. Because the trigger feels so immediate, Kwame now believes that the violence that destroyed his life is still lurking in every hallway and in every brief encounter with a male. The relentless sense that his life has been ruined fuels Kwame’s core negative appraisals. He tells himself that nothing is fair, that the world has treated him unjustly, and that the value of his life is now diminished. These beliefs drive him to shun moments of joy or warmth: he pushes away positive feelings, fearing they will betray him. When a colleague smiles or offers congratulations, Kwame avoids eye contact, feeling that the gaze might reveal a threat. He also steers clear of any confrontation, fearing that disagreement could spiral into violence. The more he holds onto these appraisals, the stronger the triggers feel, and the more the hospital smell, the presence of men, and being looked at sexually become associated with impending danger. The state of constant alertness, the endless scanning of surroundings, and the watchful eyes he perceives around him further entrench his avoidance. When the threat is heightened, he retreats into avoidance behaviors: he stops attending social events where men dominate, he declines to engage in any positive interactions at work, and he withdraws from conversations that could lead to conflict. Those very retreats reinforce his sense of danger. In the quiet moments when he feels the body on alert, the memories of the assault flood back, the auditory echoes and metallic taste returning, and the sense that the event is still unfolding. This loop makes him think his life was destroyed and that no amount of safety will ever suffice. His avoidance also serves as a bridge back to memory and threat. Every time he pushes away a pleasant feeling, a memory of a lover’s laugh turns into a recall of her abusive curses, the sound of which still rattles his ears. When he sidesteps a direct eye contact, he imagines a man’s eyes widening with threat. Each avoidance acts as a trigger that pulls him into the same state of hypervigilance he felt during the assault, ensuring the cycle continues. The cumulative effect of these patterns bleeds into his work as a parole officer. The presence of men in the courtroom, the sharp suits of prosecutors, and the male staff at his desk now feel like potential perpetrators. In the office, the very act of making eye contact with a client or negotiating a release plan triggers a surge of fear, a body on alert, and a rush of memories of the night he was beaten. Kwame has been living in this fragile equilibrium for months, his sense of safety eroded by constant self‑protection. The moment he finally sought help was when he watched a male colleague laugh with a partner and felt a sudden wave of terror, as if the laughter could trigger violence. He realized that his avoidance was isolating him from both personal and professional fulfillment. What he fears most is that if he cannot break the loop, his life will remain a series of flashes of the past, leaving him unable to experience positive feelings, to maintain eye contact, or to confront any conflict without feeling the body on alert. What he hopes for is a return to a world where the antiseptic smell of the hospital no longer wakes his heart, where the presence of men is neutral, and where his memory of the assault can rest in the past, allowing him to reclaim the life he believes he deserves.
